blocks.title: Why Train, Validation, and Test Splits matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A subscription churn model needs splits that predict future users rather than memorize the past. The learner's job is not to memorize Train, Validation, and Test Splits; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved test result remains stable after launch.

Running case: time-aware split plan with train, validation, and final test partitions. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson keeps concrete objects on the page: a real request, the information the system can see, the decision it makes, the output it returns, and the check that catches a wrong answer.

items.text: Product framing: Train, Validation, and Test Splits matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Train, Validation, and Test Splits matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure test result remains stable after launch on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: time-aware split plan with train, validation, and final test partitions

spans.text: Scenario: A subscription churn model needs splits that predict future users rather than memorize the past. The team wants to improve test result remains stable after launch, but it has already seen this failure: random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions.
Here is the whole worked artifact in one place. Read it as a complete example, not as disconnected tips.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Dataset: 40,000 subscription accounts with billing events, support tickets, product activity, and a label for churn in the next 30 days. The trap is leakage or a model that memorizes past quirks.

Artifact: time-aware split plan with train, validation, and final test partitions. It states the target, split strategy, feature rules, baseline model, validation metric, slice checks, and the failure test for test result remains stable after launch.
Worked output: train on January to April, validate on May, test on June; exclude features created after the prediction date; compare a simple baseline before adding complexity.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: ML reviewer. Context: A subscription churn model needs splits that predict future users rather than memorize the past. Task: write the modeling card for time-aware split plan with train, validation, and final test partitions. Include target, split, baseline, leakage checks, validation metric, slice checks, and rollback trigger. Output: {target, data_split, baseline, metrics, leakage_checks, risks}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Train, Validation, and Test Splits to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

Mechanism means tracing how data becomes features, how a model learns signal, and how validation estimates future performance.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to time-aware split plan with train, validation, and final test partitions: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: test result remains stable after launch becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Train, Validation, and Test Splits design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: The validation split leaks future information or near-duplicates from training.
The aggregate metric improves while an important user segment gets worse.
Feature freshness differs between training and serving.
The broad warning sign: test result remains stable after launch gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.title: Runnable check: detect a validation gap
blocks.code:
# Train Validation and Test Splits: tiny generalization diagnostic.
train_error = [0.04, 0.05, 0.05]
validation_error = [0.18, 0.19, 0.20]

def avg(xs):
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)

gap = avg(validation_error) - avg(train_error)
print(round(gap, 2))
print("do not ship" if gap > 0.10 else "continue")

spans.text: This is a runnable miniature, not the whole production system. It makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision rule, output, and a check related to random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions.

Does the artifact show input, evidence or state, decision, output, and owner?
Can you measure test result remains stable after launch on realistic cases?
Does a test reproduce this failure: random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions?
Is the next rung clear after the first reliable version?

capstone.prompt: Create a one-page release-ready plan for time-aware split plan with train, validation, and final test partitions. Include: the user problem, realistic input, mechanism, design choice, runnable or reviewable check, metric (test result remains stable after launch), failure case (random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions), owner, and the next rung after this lesson.
